title: From predictions to prescriptions in multistage optimization problems
contribution: Carries the predictive-to-prescriptive weighting into finite-horizon multistage problems: ML weights (kNN, CART, random forests) replace the conditional expectations of the dynamic program, with asymptotic optimality for all three learners, a first finite-sample regret bound for kNN, a weight-averaged SDDP algorithm, and synthetic inventory and lot-sizing runs where covariates cut cost by about 15% against SAA.
problem_entry: DA+SD (ML weights; LO/IO engines in Appendix B): multistage optimization assumes known distributions and data-driven SAA leaves out auxiliary covariates (p. 2); point predictions ignore uncertainty (p. 2) and generative-model SAA is not asymptotically optimal (p. 3); Ban et al. assume uncertainty linear in covariates (p. 4); stated as the conditional DP (2) (p. 5). Read: arXiv v1.
key_idea: Replace each conditional expectation by a weighted sum of next-stage value functions at the training observations, weights from kNN, CART or forests (pp. 6-7); SAA is w = 1/N (p. 6); nonnegative weights summing to one keep (3) a finite-scenario DP, so DP and SDDP machinery applies (pp. 7, 35-38); the theory swaps CART and Breiman forests for Wager-Athey honest, random-split, regular trees and subsampled forests (pp. 14-15, 20-21).
assumptions: T+1 stages with known transitions and costs; uncertainty independent of state and past decisions (p. 2); Markov covariates, Y_t independent of the past given X_{t-1} (pp. 5, 9); Assumptions 1-4: compact feasible sets, finite expectations, equicontinuity, compact covariate support, exponential noise tails, continuity in x (p. 9), finite Z_t allowed (p. 9); covariates uniform 'for simplicity' and Lipschitz value functions for trees and forests (p. 15); small-ball and subgaussian assumptions for the rate (p. 22); synthetic data only: 12-stage inventory control and lot sizing, 3-dimensional AR(1) covariates, factor-model demand (pp. 28-30).
proof_devices: Stage-wise telescoping: |min h - min g| <= sup|h - g| (Lemma 2) with the weights as a probability measure bounds the stage-0 error by a sum of T single-stage uniform estimation errors (pp. 11, 13-14)

Pointwise-to-uniform upgrade: countable dense subset plus equicontinuity (Lemma 4, p. 12), compactness via Bolzano-Weierstrass (Lemma 1, pp. 10-11), argmin limit points (Lemma 3, p. 11); kNN uniform consistency quoted from Biau-Devroye (Lemma 5, p. 12)

Tree leaf diameters shrink in probability: binomial lower bound on per-coordinate splits, Hoeffding and a union bound over at most N/k leaves (Lemma 6, pp. 16-17); uniform consistency by a bias-variance split (Lemma 7, pp. 17-18)

Covering-number argument (nu-net with nu = eps/(2L)) turning fixed-z bounds into sup-over-z bounds for Lipschitz functions (Lemma 8, p. 18); the weighted error shown 2L_{t+1}-Lipschitz in z (pp. 19-20)
Forest consistency by Jensen over a fixed number B of trees (Lemma 9, p. 21)

Finite-sample kNN bound: bias via the k-th neighbour distance, an eps/2-net and a binomial Hoeffding bound; variance via Biau-Devroye's (25^d/d)N^{2d} count of neighbour orderings and subgaussian Hoeffding (Lemma 10, pp. 23-25); union bound over stages and explicit constants (7) (pp. 25-27); rate O~(T/N^{1/(2d)}) for d >= 2 against O~(T/sqrt(N)) for SAA (p. 23)
Single-stage fixed-leaf forests: Wager-Athey bias theorem, McDiarmid with bounded differences 2s_N/N, Borel-Cantelli (Lemma 11 and Theorem 5, pp. 34-35)

SDDP with weight-averaged cuts, a CLT-based statistical upper bound and an eps-optimal stopping rule holding with probability >= 1 - alpha (Algorithm 1, pp. 35-37); Benders, integer optimality and Lagrangian cuts, binary expansion for mixed-integer states (p. 38)
experiments: Two synthetic 12-stage problems (inventory control, Fig. 1, p. 29; lot sizing with binary order options, Fig. 2, p. 30): out-of-sample expected cost against training size N (10 to 1000, log axis), averaged over 100 training sets (p. 28); curves SAA, kNN, RF and an 'OPT' never defined in the text (pp. 29-30), plus static-kNN/RF using only time-0 covariates (p. 31); reported cost cuts 'over 15%' (p. 29) and 'nearly 15%' (p. 31) from using covariates; not reported: CART runs, k, number of trees, whether the analyzed tree variants were used, the inventory algorithm, the basestock search, solver, hardware, run times, gaps, variability (pp. 28-31).
positioning: Extends Bertsimas-Kallus, cited as the 2014 arXiv preprint (pp. 5, 32); DP/ADP, SAA, robust DP, DRO and adaptive RO (incl. his 2011 survey) listed as neighbours without criticism (pp. 3-4); RL said to struggle with OR constraints (p. 4); only Ban et al. (2018) criticized, for its parametric assumption, and not compared (p. 4); statistics and ML said to favour estimation and prediction over prescription (p. 4); tools borrowed and named: Wager-Athey, Biau-Devroye, Shapiro, Zou et al. (pp. 12, 14-17, 23-25, 35-38).
writing: Abstract without a number: framework, asymptotic optimality 'under mild conditions', finite-sample guarantees, 'significant decrease in cost' (p. 1); section-keyed contribution list with per-learner novelty claims (pp. 5-6) and a first-to-our-knowledge finite-sample claim (p. 21); each theorem followed by a comparison paragraph (pp. 10, 21-23); 'practical tractability' (p. 6) and 'often tractable in practice' (p. 31) asserted without times; slips: the lot-sizing balance constraint copies objective terms and omits demand (p. 30), g0 counted twice in R_N (p. 22), Q0 for Q1 (p. 8).
limits_future: Stated: decision-dependent uncertainty (pricing) and efficient application variants left open (pp. 31-32); fixed-leaf forests proved only single-stage (p. 21); dimension-dependent rate penalty (pp. 22-23); O(N^T) deterministic equivalent (p. 35); basestock not optimal for lot sizing (p. 31); integer optimality cuts ineffective (p. 38). Unstated: the experiments do not say whether the analyzed learners were used (pp. 15, 21 vs 28-31); no times, gaps or variability; synthetic data only; no comparison with Ban et al. or with decision rules.

method_links.note: Step 4 (learn and decide in one model) carried to multistage: ML weights inside conditional stochastic optimization; policies scored by out-of-sample expected cost, not prediction error.

No owner, partner or current rule: covariate-blind SAA is the baseline, on synthetic data; step 5's own-cost reporting is not followed (no run times although 'practical tractability' is claimed); no field test.

The class is kept by a statistical device: probability weights keep (3) a finite-scenario DP (an LP for linear f, g), so existing machinery applies; the boundary is printed qualitatively (O(N^T), ineffective integer cuts, nonconvex lot-sizing value function) without solve times; most of the paper is asymptotic and finite-sample probability, evidence for Tension T3.

A statistical certificate (upper bound within eps of the lower bound, eps-optimal with probability >= 1 - alpha) is designed in Appendix B, but no gap is reported in the experiments and the basestock policy carries no bound (Tension T1).
A DA programme step carried by an ORC student (McCord), extending Kallus's single-stage framework with refined, reused lemmas.
In this DA paper the why-now is data availability stated qualitatively ('today's data-rich world'; data that 'continues to grow'), not a rebuilt solver-speed figure; consistent with SW5's why-then.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: SAA is the w = 1/N member of the weighted family and also the main baseline in both experiments.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: static methods adapted to dynamic problems
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The single-stage predictive-to-prescriptive weighting is carried stage by stage into a multistage DP; the lot-sizing runs separate static (time-0) from dynamic covariates.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: single-stage result lifted stage by stage
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Multistage regret bounded by a sum of T single-stage uniform estimation errors, with Bertsimas-Kallus lemmas refined and reused; one skeleton serves the kNN, tree and finite-sample proofs.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: analyzable surrogate of the practical learner
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorems proved for honest, random-split, regular trees and subsampled forests with growing leaves; the gap to standard CART and Breiman forests is stated; a separate single-stage theorem covers fixed-leaf forests.
SDDP cuts from LP or Lagrangian duals approximate the value functions and are averaged with the ML weights.

transferable: Present a learner whose weights are nonnegative and sum to one as a reweighted SAA, so that every finite-scenario solver applies and SAA is both the special case and the baseline (pp. 6-7, 35).
Telescope a multistage regret into a sum of single-stage uniform estimation errors with |min h - min g| <= sup|h - g| and Jensen over the weights (pp. 11, 13-14).

Upgrade pointwise almost-sure convergence to uniform convergence via a countable dense subset, equicontinuity and compactness; for Lipschitz objectives use a nu-net with nu = eps/(2L) (pp. 10-12, 18).

Prove results for a named analyzable variant of the practical learner (honest, random-split, regular trees), state the difference, and add a theorem for the closest practical variant where it holds (pp. 14-15, 21, 34-35).
State a finite-sample rate beside the no-covariate SAA rate and explain the dimension penalty as the price of conditioning against a better baseline (pp. 21-23).

Value-of-information ladder: no covariates (SAA), time-0 covariates (static), covariates over time (dynamic) and a full-information reference, plotted against training size and averaged over many training sets (pp. 28-31).

For integer stages, parametrize the policy by covariate-indexed basestock levels (NT parameters); in SDDP, average cut coefficients with the learned weights and use Lagrangian cuts for binary states (pp. 31, 37-38).

quotes.text: However, in general, auxiliary data has been ignored in modeling multistage problems, and this can lead to inadequate solutions.
The standard implementation of the CART algorithm does not satisfy these definitions, but it is straightforward to modify the original algorithm so that it does.

title: The price of interpretability
contribution: Defines interpretability through interpretable paths of simple model updates, derives a coherent one-parameter loss whose limits recover sparsity and greedy construction, and computes the price of interpretability as a Pareto front by weighted-sum MIO (nested OCT-type trees, SOS-1 regression) and a local-improvement heuristic, on iris, a job-prestige set and California test scores.
problem_entry: ML+IO (DA for human-in-the-loop uses): high-stakes predictions, a GDPR right to explanation and algorithm aversion demand interpretability (p. 1), but it is 'loosely defined and application-specific' (p. 1) and 'hard to define and even harder to quantify' (p. 2); post-hoc explanations and surrogates may mislead (p. 2); goal: a definition from which the accuracy trade-off can be computed (pp. 1-2). Read: arXiv v1.
key_idea: A model is the endpoint of a path of interpretable steps from a base model (pp. 3-4); a model's loss is its best path's loss (eq. 1, p. 5); path length recovers sparsity, splits and clusters (p. 5) but misses incrementality (p. 6); coherent weighted-sum losses with alpha_k = gamma^k (pp. 7-8) interpolate between complexity (gamma -> infinity) and greedy construction (gamma -> 0) (Theorem 1, p. 8); the price is the Pareto front, computed by weighted sums (Propositions 1-2, p. 9).
assumptions: Model space with a positive, possibly regularized cost c(m) (p. 2); nonempty step neighbourhoods (p. 3); bounded costs (Theorem 1), c_min <= c <= c_max and gamma >= 1 (Proposition 2) (pp. 8-9); S, m0 and gamma are modelling choices (pp. 3, 12), gamma = 1 in regression (p. 12); data: 50-point two-class iris subsample (p. 3), toy age OLS with correlation 0.9 (p. 6), 100-row job-prestige set (p. 13), California test scores 1998-1999 starting from an existing one-feature model (MSE 0.122 vs 0.095) (p. 14); no train/test split described.
proof_devices: Lift from models to paths: a model's loss is the minimum loss over paths reaching it (eq. 1, p. 5); the K-step problem generalizes best subset, best tree of given size and K-means (p. 5)
Coherence axioms: the loss depends only on the cost sequence; weak Pareto dominance; deleting the last step cannot hurt (Definition 2 and Remark, p. 7)

Theorem 1 limits: split the weighted sums at the shorter path, bound the prefix by c_max times a geometric sum and let the extra gamma^k terms dominate (gamma -> infinity); factor out gamma^K at the first lexicographic difference (gamma -> 0) (p. 8; proof pp. 17-18)
Weighted-sum scalarization gives Pareto-optimal models; the inner problem is (10) with coefficients (lambda alpha_1, ..., (1 + lambda) alpha_K) (Proposition 1, p. 9; proof p. 18)
Path-length bound K_max: the empty model's value, at most c_max, beats lambda c_min sum gamma^k (Proposition 2, p. 9; proof p. 19)
Nested-tree MIO: K OCT-type trees, tree k with exactly k active splits, monotone activation and split variables, equal thresholds by big-M-type links (14c-14f) (p. 11)
SOS-1 convex integer program for regression paths (17); outer index-sequence / inner convex QP split (18); q-step randomized local improvement (Algorithm 1) (pp. 12-13)
experiments: Toy OLS Pareto fronts for gamma = 1, 0.5 and 10, unreachable points dashed (Figs. 5-6, pp. 9-10); iris depth-2 trees by MIO, t_good with L = 9 (Fig. 7, p. 11); job prestige, K = 10: Gurobi certified optimum in 5.078 s vs local improvement 0.004 s (gap 0.02%, q = 1) and 0.019 s (gap 0.00%, q = 2) (Table 2, p. 14); California: price curve (Fig. 8), log lambda ~ -1.65, a four-step update to MSE 0.097 vs 0.095 optimal, compared with forward stagewise and a direct path (pp. 14-15); not reported: solver version, hardware, repeated heuristic runs, out-of-sample error, a user study, rival interpretability measures.
positioning: Framed by Breiman (prediction vs information, p. 1; best model at a given interpretability, p. 5); prior work sorted into interpretable model classes, sparse regression (LASSO, stagewise and LARS called 'heuristics'; his MIO work 'scalable mixed-integer approaches'), post-hoc explanations and surrogates (pp. 1-2); Lipton and Doshi-Velez-Kim for the definitional gap (p. 2); claims to generalize many approaches (p. 5) and to answer 'a central question' of the literature (p. 9); links to incremental approximation, prioritization and scoring systems (p. 12).
writing: Title echoes 'The price of robustness' [inferred]; abstract without a number: stakes, 'However' the concept is loosely defined, framework, recovered proxies, parametrized family, the 'price' in quotation marks (p. 1); worked examples before axioms (pp. 3-6), then axioms, family and limit theorem (pp. 7-8); specific hedges ('a modeling choice', 'a hard question', 'may not scale', 'application-dependent'; pp. 3, 6, 11, 12); slips: 'Bersimas' (p. 1), L_gamma for L_alpha (p. 8), undefined 'coordinate paths' (p. 9), 'interprtability' and 'Table 9a' (p. 14).
limits_future: Stated: weighted sums miss non-convex parts of the front (p. 9); MIO may not scale and exactness is often unnecessary (p. 11); exact regression only for d <= 10, K <= 10 (p. 13); each application has its own challenges, left as 'an opportunity for further research' (p. 14). Unstated: no human-subject validation (cf. p. 2), very small data, in-sample MSE only, no guidance for choosing S, m0 or gamma, no scalar price, no comparison with other interpretability measures.

method_links.note: Property named with those who want it (individuals, regulators, algorithm-averse decision makers); knobs defined; class kept (MIO for trees and regression); price curves on a toy, a benchmark and a real data set; a point picked on the curve by diminishing returns (log lambda ~ -1.65) and the choice of complexity left to a decision maker in section 5.3; the method's bad case printed (unreachable Pareto points dashed).

Two knobs, not one: gamma fixes what interpretability means and lambda traces the price; the guarantee is a limit theorem plus a path-length bound, not a solution-independent bound on the property; the price is a Pareto front with no scalar headline.

A property owned by ML and human factors written exactly as MIO (nested OCT-type trees) and an SOS-1 convex integer program (regression), opening on 'Most machine learning problems can be viewed through the lens of optimization'; boundary printed (d <= 10, K <= 10; 'may not scale').

Exact MIO used as the certificate that measures a local-improvement heuristic on a small instance (Heuristic 3), with the concession that provable optimality is often unnecessary (Tension T1); greedy forward stagewise is an in-sample opponent along the path and is priced rather than replaced: it is the gamma -> 0 limit, with its first-step virtue stated, which qualifies Taste warning sign 3.

The deployed model is the path's start m0 and the path explains the update from it (the current rule as starting point, not only as baseline); but the metric is MSE, no owner or decision is named, and nothing is field-tested.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: nest the incumbent rule as a limiting case of the priced model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Sparsity (complexity) is the gamma -> infinity limit and greedy construction the gamma -> 0 limit of L_gamma; the K-step problem generalizes best subset, best tree of a given size and K-means.
Coherence axioms (dependence on the cost sequence only, weak Pareto dominance), then the weighted family L_alpha, then the one-parameter L_gamma.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact optimum on a small solvable instance as the certificate for a heuristic
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Gurobi's certified optimum on a 100-row instance measures the local-improvement heuristic's time and gap (0.02% and 0.00%).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: define the property on the construction path, not only on the endpoint
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Interpretability is a loss on paths of interpretable steps; a model inherits the loss of its best path; equal-complexity trees are separated by their intermediate costs.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: incumbent model as the start of an explainable update path
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The California study starts the path at an existing one-feature model and reaches a near-optimal model in four readable coefficient changes.

transferable: Define a vague property through a step neighbourhood S and a base model m0: put the loss on paths and give each model the loss of its best path (pp. 3-5).
Axioms first, then a weighted family that satisfies them, then a one-parameter member (alpha_k = gamma^k) whose limits provably recover the field's proxies (pp. 7-8, 17-18).
Compute a price as a Pareto front by weighted-sum scalarization, bound the number of subproblems, and draw the non-convex parts the scalarization cannot reach (pp. 9-10, 18-19).
Encode a nested sequence of models as K coupled copies with monotone activation and equal-split linking constraints (p. 11).
Split a path problem into an outer combinatorial index sequence and an inner convex QP; improve by re-optimizing q randomly chosen steps over all index choices (p. 13).
Calibrate a heuristic against the exact MIO on a small real instance and print time and gap side by side (Table 2, p. 14).
Set the step weights to the probabilities that a decision maker picks complexity k (alpha_k = p_k) to obtain a nested family that minimizes expected cost over that choice (p. 12).
Start the path at the deployed model, so that an update reads as a short sequence of coefficient changes with the MSE after each (pp. 14-15).
coauthors: Arthur Delarue (MIT ORC), Patrick Jaillet (MIT EECS), Sebastien Martin (MIT ORC)

quotes.text: However, the concept of interpretability remains loosely defined and application-specific.

In general, mixed-integer optimization formulations such as (14) may not scale. However, in many cases a provably optimal solution is not necessary and scalable heuristics such as local improvement may be employed.
